title: Charity is friendship (ST II-II.23.1)
hook: Thomas calls charity friendship with God

segments.voice: Yesterday, temperance: the right measure of the body's pleasures, which Thomas says gives a life its beauty. Your line was enough is beautiful. Where did you find enough? Day one thousand one hundred seventy-three.

"I will not now call you servants." Jesus says it at the Last Supper, in John's Gospel, the night before he dies. "But I have called you friends." A servant does what he's told without being let in on the plan. A friend gets told things. Thomas Aquinas takes that one word, friends, very seriously. When he comes to charity, the love Paul calls the greatest of faith, hope and charity, the love that never falls away, the first question he asks is not whether it's a feeling, or a duty, or a kind of kindness. He asks whether charity is friendship. And his answer is today's title.

Thomas borrows a definition of friendship from Aristotle, and it has three parts. First, not every love is friendship. People love wine, Thomas says, but nobody is friends with wine. You want it for yourself; you don't wish it well. Friendship means wanting good for the other, for their sake. Second, that good will has to go both ways. A one-sided love is not yet a friendship. Third, friends share something: a life, a work, a table. Friendship is built on that sharing. Now Thomas lays this over God. Does God wish us well, for our sake? Yes. Is the love returned? It can be. And what's shared? Thomas says God shares his own happiness with us, and he points to Paul, in the Douay-Rheims: "God is faithful: by whom you are called unto the fellowship of his Son." Fellowship is the shared thing. So charity, for Thomas, is friendship between a person and God. Here's what makes it bold. Aristotle, the very teacher Thomas is borrowing from, doubted that friendship could stretch across a gap as wide as the one between people and gods. And Thomas raises a sharp objection against himself: friends live together, and we don't live with God. His answer is that we do, already, in part. He quotes Paul again: "But our conversation is in heaven." In that old English, conversation means the way you live, where you belong. It's begun here and finished later. One more turn. Because a friend loves what belongs to the friend, Thomas says charity reaches everyone God loves, even enemies. You love them the way you'd care for a friend's children, for the friend's sake. Charity, then, is not a mood. It's a friendship with a wide circle.
screen: `NOBODY IS FRIENDS WITH WINE.` · `GOOD WILL, BOTH WAYS, SOMETHING SHARED.` · `GOD SHARES HIS HAPPINESS.` · `BEGUN HERE, FINISHED LATER.` · then, large: `I HAVE CALLED YOU FRIENDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: talk the way friends talk. Settle, and breathe. Friends don't make speeches. They say what happened, what's bothering them, what made them laugh. If you pray, spend the time talking with God like that: plainly, about today, and then be quiet for a bit, the way you would with a friend. If you don't pray, bring to mind one real friendship, and notice its three parts in it: wishing them well, being wished well back, and the thing you share. The bell holds the time.
Charity is friendship. For Thomas, charity is not only kindness. It's a friendship between a person and God, built on the happiness God shares. Today's word.
Your line: friendship with god. Today, once, tell God or a friend something true about your day, the way friends do, without dressing it up. Day one thousand one hundred seventy-three.

howItsDone: Catholics speak of charity as the greatest of the theological virtues, and the Catechism, following Thomas, describes it as the virtue by which people love God above all things and their neighbor for the love of God, and, with St. Teresa of Avila, describes prayer as a close sharing between friends.

fork.setup: an objector tells Thomas that friends live together, and we don't live with God, so charity can't be friendship. what does Thomas answer?
options: we already live with God in part, and fully later.
say friendship doesn't need any shared life.
fork.reveal: Thomas quotes Paul, "our conversation is in heaven": the shared life is begun now and finished later.

original.note: Latin, the language Thomas wrote in: charity, the love Thomas calls friendship with God.

trapdoor: what you thought: charity means giving money away.
what it means: for Thomas, charity is friendship with God: good will both ways, built on the happiness God shares.
what a scholar hears: Thomas fits Aristotle's definition of friendship to God, though Aristotle doubted friendship could cross that gap.

notes: All Aquinas is paraphrased. Check: not every love is friendship (the wine/horse example), friendship requires benevolence, mutual love, and a communicatio (II-II.23.1); God's communication of his happiness as the basis, citing 1 Cor 1:9; the objection that friends live together, answered with Phil 3:20 (ad 1); charity extends to enemies as a friend's children (ad 2).
'Greatest of the virtues' and 'never falls away' paraphrase 1 Corinthians 13:8 and 13:13; confirm.
Aristotle's doubt that friendship can cross the gap to the gods paraphrases Nicomachean Ethics VIII.7; Thomas's question cites Aristotle but does not raise this point himself. Confirm the framing.
Douay-Rheims wording to confirm: John 15:15 (two fragments), 1 Corinthians 1:9 (fragment), Philippians 3:20.
'Conversation' glossed as 'the way you live, where you belong' (archaic sense); confirm.
howItsDone paraphrases CCC 1822 and CCC 2709 (Teresa of Avila on prayer as a close sharing between friends).
Editor pass: 'greatest of the virtues' narrowed to Paul's 'greatest of faith, hope and charity' (1 Cor 13:13); cut the dear/carus etymology from the original note; varied the fork frame.
